html:
The 1918 influenza pandemic, often called the Spanish flu, killed more people in India than in any other country: probably between 12 and 17 million, perhaps five percent of the population.

The virus arrived by ship at Bombay in mid 1918, likely with troops coming home from the First World War. A mild first wave was followed in September by a far deadlier second wave that swept along the railways from the ports into the countryside. Most victims were young adults. In some districts so many died that the rivers were clogged with bodies because there was no wood to burn them.

The monsoon had also failed that year, so food was short and prices high, which made people weaker. The colonial health service was small and did little.

Bombay had suffered from the plague two decades earlier, and the two disasters fed anger against British rule in the years just before Gandhi's first mass campaigns. The death toll in India was a large share of the world total, and dwarfs that of places like Samoa. A century later India faced Covid.
sum: The 1918 influenza pandemic, often called the Spanish flu, killed more people in India than in any other country: probably between 12 and 17 million, perhaps five percent of the population.
